# rv32iv: a RISC-V processor with a vector unit, generated by an AI design flow

**In one paragraph.** `rv32iv` is a small computer on a chip (a *system-on-chip*, SoC). Its main part is a processor
that executes the open **RISC-V** instruction set, extended with a **vector unit** that performs the same arithmetic on
16 small numbers at once. Around it are two memories, a block of control/status registers and a serial port. The
example task is to recognize a handwritten digit (0 to 9) with a small neural network. The design was not written by
hand: a person wrote one short intent document, and the multi-agent chip design platform **Q3TUI** produced the
specification, the hardware description, the tests, the program, the constraints and the reports.

How to read this file: section 1 explains every term and abbreviation used afterwards; sections 2 and 3 tell where the
design comes from and how it was made; sections 4 to 6 describe the hardware and the instructions in detail; sections
7 to 9 describe what it can be used for; section 10 gives the results and what they do not prove; sections 11 to 13 are
reference (folders, how to rerun, limits).

## 1. Glossary: every term and abbreviation

### 1.1 Processor and instruction set

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **ISA** (instruction set architecture) | The list of instructions a processor understands and what each one does. Software is written against the ISA, hardware implements it |
| **RISC-V** | An open, royalty-free ISA. It has a small mandatory base and optional **extensions** that are named by letters or by `Z...` names |
| **RV32I** | The RISC-V base ISA with **32**-bit registers and **I**nteger instructions. About 40 instructions: arithmetic, logic, shifts, loads, stores, branches, jumps |
| **Zmmul** | The extension that adds only **multiplication** (`mul`) without division. It is the "M" extension without `div` and `rem`, so the multiplier is small and there is no slow divider |
| **Zve32x** | The **embedded profile of the RISC-V Vector extension**: integer vector instructions only (no floating point), element width up to 32 bits (ELEN = 32). This design implements a subset of it |
| **Vector extension** | RISC-V instructions that apply one operation to a whole **vector** (a row of numbers) in one instruction (this is also called SIMD: single instruction, multiple data) |
| **Register** | A fast storage cell inside the processor. A **scalar register** holds one number; a **vector register** holds a row of numbers |
| **x0 ... x31** | The 32 scalar registers of RV32I. `x0` always reads 0 and ignores writes |
| **v0 ... v31** | The 32 vector registers of the vector extension |
| **PC** (program counter) | The register that holds the address of the instruction being fetched |
| **Immediate** | A constant that is written inside the instruction itself |
| **Opcode** | The field of an instruction that tells which kind of instruction it is |
| **Funct3, funct6, funct7** | Extra fields next to the opcode that select the exact operation in a group |
| **Sign extension / zero extension** | Widening a number by copying its top (sign) bit / by filling with zeros. Used when a byte or half-word is loaded into a 32-bit register |
| **Word / half-word / byte** | 32 / 16 / 8 bits of data |
| **Aligned / misaligned** | An access is aligned when its address is a multiple of its size (a 4-byte word at an address divisible by 4) |
| **NOP** | An instruction that does nothing |
| **Trap / exception** | A change of control that a processor makes on an error or special event. This core has **no traps**: an error halts it |
| **CSR (RISC-V sense)** | A *control and status register* that special RISC-V instructions read and write. This core has none. (The other CSR, in 4.4, is a block of memory-mapped registers) |
| **Pipeline** | Splitting an instruction into stages so that several instructions are in progress at the same time |
| **IF / ID / EX / MEM / WB** | The five pipeline stages: **I**nstruction **F**etch, **I**nstruction **D**ecode, **EX**ecute, **MEM**ory access, **W**rite **B**ack |
| **Hazard** | A situation where the next instruction needs a result that is not ready yet. The core solves it by **forwarding** (passing the result directly), a **stall** (waiting) or a **bubble** (an empty slot) |
| **Flush** | Throwing away the instructions that were fetched after a taken branch because they should not run |
| **Branch prediction (not-taken)** | The core guesses that a branch is not taken and keeps fetching the next instruction; if the guess is wrong it flushes (about 2 cycles lost) |

### 1.2 Vector and neural-network terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **VPU** (vector processing unit) | The hardware block that executes the vector instructions |
| **VLEN** | The width of one vector register in bits. Here 128 bits = 16 bytes |
| **SEW** (selected element width) | The width of one element: 8, 16 or 32 bits. 128 / 8 = 16 elements of 8 bits per register |
| **LMUL** | Register grouping factor: use 1, 2, 4 or 8 registers as one longer vector. Here only **LMUL = 1** is legal |
| **ELEN** | The widest element the hardware supports (32 bits here) |
| **vl** | The number of elements the next vector instruction works on (vector length). It is set by `vsetvli` |
| **VLMAX** | The largest possible `vl` = VLEN / SEW × LMUL. At SEW = 8 it is 16 |
| **AVL** | The number of elements the program still wants to process (application vector length). `vl = min(AVL, VLMAX)` |
| **Lane** | One parallel slice of the vector unit. 4 lanes of 32 bits process 128 bits per step |
| **Tail** | The elements of a vector register beyond `vl`. They are left unchanged |
| **Widening / narrowing** | An operation whose result is twice as wide as its inputs (INT8 × INT8 → INT16), or the reverse |
| **Saturation (clip)** | When a result does not fit the target width, it is replaced by the nearest largest or smallest value instead of wrapping around |
| **Reduction** | Combining all the elements of a vector into one value, for example their sum |
| **INT8 / INT16 / INT32** | Signed integers of 8, 16 and 32 bits (INT8 range −128 to 127) |
| **Dot product** | The sum of the products of two lists of numbers: a₀b₀ + a₁b₁ + ... It is the core operation of a neural network |
| **MAC** | Multiply-accumulate: one multiplication followed by an addition |
| **Neural network, neuron, layer** | A model made of layers; each neuron computes a dot product of its inputs with its weights, adds a bias and applies an activation |
| **MLP** | Multi-layer perceptron: layers of neurons, each fully connected to the previous layer |
| **Weights, bias** | The numbers learned during training. Weights multiply the inputs, the bias is added after the sum |
| **ReLU** | The activation max(0, x): negative values become 0 |
| **Logits** | The raw output numbers of the last layer, one per class. The largest one is the answer |
| **argmax** | The index of the largest element |
| **Inference** | Using a trained network to classify new data (as opposed to **training**) |
| **Quantization, requantization** | Replacing real numbers by small integers (here INT8) to save memory and hardware; requantization scales a result back to INT8 after a sum |
| **Golden model** | A trusted program (here in Python) that computes the exact expected result so that the hardware can be compared bit by bit |
| **MNIST** | A public set of handwritten digit images, 28 × 28 pixels, grey scale, digits 0 to 9 |

### 1.3 Chip, memory and bus terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **SoC** | System-on-chip: processor, memories and peripherals on one chip |
| **RTL** | Register-transfer level: the hardware description (SystemVerilog files `.sv`) from which a chip or FPGA is built |
| **SystemVerilog** | The language the RTL is written in |
| **Module** | One hardware block in RTL. Names here start with `m_` (for example `m_alu`) |
| **FSM** | Finite-state machine: a block that moves through a fixed list of states |
| **IMEM / DMEM** | Instruction memory (the program) / data memory (weights, image, results) |
| **SRAM, M20K** | On-chip memory; M20K is the 20-kilobit memory block of Intel FPGAs |
| **MMIO** | Memory-mapped input/output: registers that the program reads and writes like memory, at addresses in a special region |
| **CSR block (hardware sense)** | The block of MMIO control/status registers `m_soc_csr` (start, status, result, cycle count, UART). Generated by the APB-CSR-Generator tool |
| **APB / APB4** | AMBA Advanced Peripheral Bus, version 4: a simple bus for slow registers. `PSEL`, `PENABLE` start a transfer, `PREADY` ends it, `PSTRB` selects bytes, `PSLVERR` signals an error |
| **UART** | Universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter: a serial port. **8N1** = 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit. **Baud** = bits per second; the **divisor** sets it from the clock |
| **Clock domain, CDC** | A set of logic on one clock / a signal crossing between two clocks. This design has one clock and no crossing |
| **Reset (asynchronous assert, synchronous release)** | Puts the design in its starting state. It can start at any time but ends in step with the clock (`m_rst_sync`) |
| **Host** | The outside controller (a PC or a testbench) that loads the memories and starts a run |
| **ASIC / FPGA** | A custom chip / a re-programmable chip. The design is prototyped on an FPGA (Intel **Arria 10**) |
| **ALM, DSP block, register** | FPGA resources: adaptive logic module (logic cell), multiplier block, flip-flop |

### 1.4 Flow, verification and timing terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **VLSIT** | The organization name used in names and headers (`VLSIT - Q3TUI`) |
| **Q3TUI, Q3CORE** | The AI-driven ASIC design flow (a terminal user interface with several agents) and its engine that produced this example |
| **Agent** | An AI program that does one job in the flow (write the spec, write RTL, fix a test) |
| **Intent** | The one short document written by a person that describes the goal |
| **Spec** | Specification: the detailed description of the design with numbered requirements |
| **REQ-nnn, TC-nnn** | A requirement number / a test case number |
| **DV** | Design verification: proving by tests that the design works |
| **Testbench, DUT** | The test program around the design / the design under test |
| **Lint, style lint** | Automatic checks of code for errors and rule violations. **Verilator** and **Verible** are the lint tools used |
| **VCS** | A commercial hardware simulator |
| **Spike** | The official RISC-V instruction-set simulator, used as a reference |
| **Plusarg** | A `+NAME=value` option given to the simulator on the command line |
| **SDC** | Synopsys Design Constraints: a file that gives the clock and input/output timing |
| **Synthesis, place-and-route** | Turning RTL into gates / placing and wiring them. Only synthesis was run here |
| **STA, WNS, WHS, TNS, Fmax** | Static timing analysis. **Worst negative slack** (setup) / **worst hold slack** / **total negative slack**. Slack is the spare time of the slowest path; positive means timing is met. **Fmax** is the highest clock the design can run |
| **Triage** | Finding the cause of a failure and deciding what to fix |
| **PPA** | Power, performance, area |
| **DFT, UPF, ECC** | Design for test, power-intent format, error-correcting code (not used here) |

## 2. Origin: where the design comes from

| Item | Content |
|---|---|
| Generator | **Q3TUI**, the multi-agent chip design platform of the Q3TUI and Q3CORE ASIC AI Design flow; generated files name `VLSIT - Q3TUI` as author |
| Human input | One document, `spec/intent.md` (615 lines, draft v0.2, "RISC-V + VPU for MNIST image recognition"): goal and scope, the network, the vector instructions, the CPU, the memory map, the register plan, the host load port, the tools and the open questions |
| Rules the flow had to follow | The VLSIT RTL design rules v2: naming (`m_` modules, `i_`/`o_` ports, `PARA_`/`LPARA_` parameters), one module per file, a structural top, no `initial` or `$readmemh` in RTL, no `signed` types; the register block is generated by the APB-CSR-Generator tool |
| Run mode | `auto_approve: true` and `auto_answer: true` in `q3tui.yaml`: review gates were approved automatically and every open question was answered with the default the agent proposed |
| Date of the run | 2026-10-31 (timestamps in `schemas/dv_evidence.json` and `reviews/*.json`) |
| Tools | VCS (simulation), Verible and Verilator (lint), Quartus Prime Pro 25.1 (FPGA synthesis), VC Static, RISC-V GCC 14.2 (compiler), Spike (reference); the list is in `config/tools.json` |

**Why this design.** It is a complete, non-trivial example for an AI flow: a pipelined processor, an accelerator with its own
control, memories, a generated register block, a serial port, firmware and a numeric workload whose result can be checked
bit by bit.

## 3. How it was made

Q3TUI works in four flows. Each flow is a chain of steps; an agent does a step, tools check it, and a failure goes to a
triage agent that fixes the RTL or the testbench and tries again.

| Flow | Steps | What each step does | Result in this folder |
|---|---|---|---|
| **spec** | spec → parse → config | Write the 21-section specification from the intent; split it into numbered requirements; derive parameters and modules | `spec/spec.md`, `schemas/structured_spec.json` (87 requirements), `schemas/final_config.json` |
| **rtl** | rules → csr → rtl → format → style_lint → smoke | Load the coding rules; generate the register block; write the modules; format; check rules; run a smoke simulation | 38 modules (7,306 lines) in `src/rtl/` |
| **dv** | testplan → tb → prepare → simulate | Plan 60 tests; write the testbench; build firmware and golden data; simulate and triage failures | `schemas/test_plan.json`, `src/tb/`, `src/sw/`, `reports/dv_test_results.md` |
| **fpga** | fpga_port → sdc → fpga_synth → timing_util_report → ppa_optimize | Adapt memories to Arria 10; write the SDC; synthesize; read timing and area; optimize | `constraints/sdc/`, `schemas/fpga_synth.json`, `schemas/ppa_report.json` |

**Questions and answers.** When the specification does not decide something, the agent asks a structured question with a
default and two or three options, each with its impact. This run asked 47 questions (`schemas/questions/`):

| Step | Questions | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| spec | 7 | latency of `vwredsum` (multi-cycle), rounding of `vnclip` (round to nearest, up), partial MMIO writes (reach APB, `PSLVERR` sets `sts.err`) |
| parse | 2 | temporary register map; Quartus version and FPGA part |
| csr | 4 | register offsets, bit positions, `uart_tx.send` as a self-clearing field |
| rtl | 26 | port lists the spec did not give (`m_pc_gen`, `m_alu`, `m_branch_unit`), who owns the halt flag, priority of stall versus redirect |
| prepare | 2 | synthetic placeholder weights; how the MNIST options reach the simulator |
| simulate | 6 | failure triage (below) |

With `auto_answer` all were closed with the default. The six `simulate` questions were blocking and had no options; all got
the answer "keep the spec as written and treat the failing side as the bug". They were testbench faults (a test that overwrote
its own data, queues not cleared between baud rates, missing plusargs, a bus monitor that ignored reset), not RTL faults.

## 4. The hardware

### 4.1 Block diagram

```
                    +--------------------------------- m_soc_top ----------------------------------+
  i_start_req ----> |                                                                               |
                    |  +-----------+  vector instr, rs1/rs2   +--------------------+                |
                    |  | m_cpu_top | -----------------------> | m_vpu_top          |                |
                    |  | RV32I +   | <----------------------- | VLEN 128, 4 lanes  |                |
                    |  | Zmmul     |  done / rd data          | 32 vector regs     |                |
                    |  | 5 stages  |                          +---------+----------+                |
                    |  +-----+-----+                                    |                           |
                    |        |   m_soc_bus: address decode, mux         |  128-bit memory port      |
                    |  +-----+-------------------------------------------+---------+                |
  i_ld_* (host) --> |  | m_host_ld: 2:1 DMEM mux + IMEM write while the core is in reset |         |
                    |  +--------------------+-----------------------------+----------+              |
                    |   m_imem 32 KB        |   m_dmem 256 KB                                       |
                    |  +--------------------+---------+                                             |
                    |  | m_apb_master -> m_soc_csr (APB4 CSR) + m_uart ---------> o_uart_tx         |
                    |  +--------------------------------------------------------> o_result_label,   |
                    |        m_rst_sync (reset synchronizer)                       o_sts_done, o_halt|
                    +-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

One clock `i_clk_core` and one reset `i_rst_n_core` (active low: the design is in reset while it is 0). Port names start with
`i_` for inputs and `o_` for outputs.

### 4.2 Scalar core (`m_cpu_top`)

| Stage | What happens | Modules |
|---|---|---|
| IF | The PC addresses the instruction memory; next PC is PC + 4, a branch target or a jump target | `m_pc_gen`, `m_imem` |
| ID | The instruction is decoded, the immediate is built, two registers are read | `m_cpu_dec`, `m_imm_gen`, `m_regfile` |
| EX | The ALU computes, the multiplier multiplies, a branch is decided | `m_alu`, `m_mul`, `m_branch_unit` |
| MEM | A load or store goes to the data memory or, for MMIO addresses, over APB to the register block and the UART | `m_lsu`, `m_soc_bus` |
| WB | The result is written to the register file | `m_mem_wb_reg` |

| Situation | What the core does (`m_hazard_unit`) |
|---|---|
| Result needed by the next instruction | Forwarding from EX/MEM and MEM/WB, and a write-to-read bypass in the register file |
| A load followed at once by its use | One bubble |
| A branch or jump is taken | Decided in EX; the two younger instructions are flushed |
| A vector instruction is running | The whole pipeline waits for the vector unit's `done` |
| Error | An illegal instruction or `ebreak` halts the core: `o_halt` = 1 (and `o_err_illegal` = 1 for an illegal instruction). There are no interrupts or traps |

After reset the PC is `0x0000_0000`. A wrong-path instruction that is flushed before it commits has no effect, even if it is illegal.

### 4.3 Vector unit (`m_vpu_top`)

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| VLEN | 128 bits (`PARA_VLEN` can be 128 or 256; 128 is the verified setting) |
| Lanes | 4 lanes of 32 bits (`PARA_LANE_COUNT` can be 1, 2, 4 or 8; 4 is verified) |
| SEW / LMUL | 8, 16, 32 bits / LMUL = 1 only |
| Registers | 32 vector registers `v0`..`v31` of 128 bits |
| Execution | One vector instruction at a time, no overlap; every instruction passes six sequencer states (idle, decode, read, execute, write back, done) so it takes at least 5 cycles |

Modules: `m_vpu_if` (handshake with the core), `m_vpu_dec` (decode), `m_vpu_csr` (holds the element width and `vl`),
`m_vpu_ctrl` (sequencer state machine), `m_vpu_regfile` (vector registers), `m_vpu_lsu` (128-bit memory port),
`m_vpu_lane` × 4 (each with `m_lane_alu`, `m_lane_mul`, `m_lane_narrow`), `m_vpu_reduce` (adder tree across lanes),
`m_vpu_perf` (counts cycles of the inference).

### 4.4 Memories, address map and registers

| Region | Address | Size | Content |
|---|---|---|---|
| Instruction memory | `0x0000_0000` | 32 KB | The program (`m_imem`, 1-cycle read) |
| Data memory | `0x1000_0000` | 256 KB | `[W1 | b1 | W2 | b2 | image | act1 | logits | stack]` (weights layer 1, bias 1, weights layer 2, bias 2, input image, hidden activations, outputs, stack), 16-byte aligned (`m_dmem`) |
| MMIO | `0x2000_0000` | 4 KB | The CSR block and the UART |

A data access to the instruction-memory range is treated as unmapped (reads 0, writes ignored). An access to an unused MMIO
offset reads 0 and changes nothing.

Control/status registers (CSR block, offset from `0x2000_0000`; only full 32-bit aligned writes are accepted, a partial write
gives the APB error `PSLVERR`, which sets `sts.err`):

| Offset | Register | Fields | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | `ctrl` | `start` | The pin `i_start_req` sets it; the program clears it |
| `0x04` | `sts` | `busy`, `done`, `err` | Progress flags and a sticky error flag (illegal instruction or bus error; cleared by writing 1) |
| `0x08` | `result` | `label[3:0]` | The predicted digit |
| `0x0C` | `cycles` | `cnt[31:0]` | Cycles of the last vector-unit run (read only) |
| `0x10` | `uart_tx` | `data[7:0]`, `send`, `busy` | Send one byte; `m_uart` clears `send` when it takes the byte |
| `0x14` | `uart_cfg` | `baud_div[15:0]` | Baud divisor, reset value `0x06C8`; 200 MHz / 115,200 baud is about 1,736 |

**Host load port** (`i_ld_*`, `o_ld_rd_data`, module `m_host_ld`). While the core is held in reset, a host can write the
program to the instruction memory, write weights and image to the data memory, and read results back, with no handshake
(a read returns after one cycle). The port must be off (`i_ld_en` = 0) whenever the core runs.

## 5. The RISC-V scalar instruction set (RV32I + Zmmul)

### 5.1 Concepts in a few lines

RISC-V is a **load/store** architecture: arithmetic works only on registers; only loads and stores touch memory.
There are 32 registers of 32 bits. Each instruction is 32 bits wide and has one of six formats.

| Format | Used by | Fields (high bit → low bit) |
|---|---|---|
| **R** | register-register arithmetic | funct7, rs2, rs1, funct3, rd, opcode |
| **I** | immediate arithmetic, loads, `jalr` | imm[11:0], rs1, funct3, rd, opcode |
| **S** | stores | imm[11:5], rs2, rs1, funct3, imm[4:0], opcode |
| **B** | conditional branches | imm[12\|10:5], rs2, rs1, funct3, imm[4:1\|11], opcode |
| **U** | `lui`, `auipc` | imm[31:12], rd, opcode |
| **J** | `jal` | imm[20\|10:1\|11\|19:12], rd, opcode |

`rd` = destination register, `rs1`, `rs2` = source registers.

Register names used in the examples (RISC-V calling convention):

| Registers | Name | Role |
|---|---|---|
| x0 | zero | always 0 |
| x1 | ra | return address |
| x2 | sp | stack pointer |
| x5-x7, x28-x31 | t0-t6 | temporaries |
| x8, x9, x18-x27 | s0-s11 | saved registers |
| x10-x17 | a0-a7 | arguments and results |

### 5.2 The instructions this core executes

`x[rs1]` means the value of register rs1; `sext` = sign-extend; `M[a]` = memory at address a.

**Arithmetic and logic, register-register (R format)**

| Instruction | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `add rd, rs1, rs2` | rd = rs1 + rs2 | `add a0, a1, a2` |
| `sub rd, rs1, rs2` | rd = rs1 − rs2 | `sub a0, a1, a2` |
| `and`, `or`, `xor` | bitwise AND, OR, exclusive OR | `xor t0, t1, t2` |
| `sll rd, rs1, rs2` | shift left logical by rs2[4:0], zeros enter | `sll a0, a1, a2` |
| `srl rd, rs1, rs2` | shift right logical by rs2[4:0], zeros enter | `srl a0, a1, a2` |
| `sra rd, rs1, rs2` | shift right arithmetic, the sign bit enters | `sra a0, a1, a2` |
| `slt rd, rs1, rs2` | rd = 1 if rs1 < rs2 (signed), else 0 | `slt t0, a0, a1` |
| `sltu rd, rs1, rs2` | rd = 1 if rs1 < rs2 (unsigned), else 0 | `sltu t0, a0, a1` |

**Arithmetic and logic with an immediate (I format)**

| Instruction | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `addi rd, rs1, imm` | rd = rs1 + sext(imm12). `addi rd, x0, imm` loads a small constant; `addi x0,x0,0` is the NOP | `addi sp, sp, -16` |
| `andi`, `ori`, `xori` | bitwise with a 12-bit immediate | `andi a0, a0, 0xFF` |
| `slli`, `srli`, `srai` | shifts by a constant of 0 to 31 | `slli a0, a0, 2` (× 4) |
| `slti`, `sltiu` | set-less-than with an immediate | `sltiu a0, a0, 1` (a0 == 0) |

**Constants and addresses (U format)**

| Instruction | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `lui rd, imm20` | rd = imm20 << 12 (loads the upper 20 bits) | `lui a0, 0x10000` → `0x1000_0000` |
| `auipc rd, imm20` | rd = PC + (imm20 << 12) (PC-relative address) | `auipc t0, 0` |

A 32-bit constant is built with `lui` followed by `addi`.

**Jumps and branches (J, I and B formats)**

| Instruction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `jal rd, label` | rd = PC + 4; PC = PC + offset (call or jump) |
| `jalr rd, rs1, imm` | rd = PC + 4; PC = (rs1 + imm) with bit 0 cleared (return, indirect call) |
| `beq rs1, rs2, label` | jump if rs1 == rs2 |
| `bne rs1, rs2, label` | jump if rs1 != rs2 |
| `blt`, `bge` | jump if rs1 < rs2 / rs1 ≥ rs2 (signed) |
| `bltu`, `bgeu` | the same, unsigned |

A branch is decided in the EX stage. A taken branch costs about two cycles (flush), a not-taken branch costs none.

**Loads and stores (I and S formats)**

| Instruction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `lb rd, imm(rs1)` | load 1 byte, sign-extended |
| `lbu rd, imm(rs1)` | load 1 byte, zero-extended |
| `lh rd, imm(rs1)` | load 2 bytes, sign-extended |
| `lhu rd, imm(rs1)` | load 2 bytes, zero-extended |
| `lw rd, imm(rs1)` | load 4 bytes |
| `sb rs2, imm(rs1)` | store the low byte of rs2 |
| `sh rs2, imm(rs1)` | store the low 2 bytes of rs2 |
| `sw rs2, imm(rs1)` | store 4 bytes |

The address is `rs1 + imm`. A **misaligned** load or store does **not trap** in this core: a misaligned load returns
`word >> (8 × addr[1:0])` with zero fill and then the normal sign or zero extension; bytes outside the word are dropped.
Accesses to the register block (MMIO) must be full aligned words (`lw`, `sw`), otherwise `PSLVERR` is raised.

**Multiplication (Zmmul)**

| Instruction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `mul rd, rs1, rs2` | rd = the low 32 bits of rs1 × rs2 |

**System**

| Instruction | Behavior in this core |
|---|---|
| `fence` | executes as a NOP (there is one memory and no other core) |
| `ebreak` | stops the core: `o_halt` = 1; the program uses it to finish |

**Illegal in this core (they halt it and raise `o_err_illegal`):** `div`, `divu`, `rem`, `remu`, `mulh`, `mulhsu`, `mulhu`,
`ecall`, all CSR instructions (`csrrw`, ...), atomic, floating-point and compressed instructions, and every unsupported
vector form. Division is not needed because the requantization of the neural network is a shift. Firmware must not divide
by a variable.

### 5.3 A small example

Sum the 10 words starting at `0x1000_0000` and keep the result in `a0`:

```
        lui   t0, 0x10000          # t0 = 0x1000_0000  (address of the data)
        addi  t1, x0, 10           # t1 = 10           (counter)
        addi  a0, x0, 0            # a0 = 0            (sum)
loop:   lw    t2, 0(t0)            # t2 = M[t0]
        add   a0, a0, t2           # sum += t2
        addi  t0, t0, 4            # next word
        addi  t1, t1, -1           # counter -= 1
        bne   t1, x0, loop         # repeat while counter != 0
        ebreak                     # stop
```

---

## 6. The RISC-V vector instruction set (Zve32x subset)

### 6.1 Concepts

A vector instruction works on many elements at once. Three settings decide how:

- **SEW** (element width): 8, 16 or 32 bits.
- **LMUL**: register grouping; here always 1 (one register per vector).
- **vl**: how many elements the next instruction processes. `vsetvli` computes `vl = min(AVL, VLMAX)`.

With VLEN = 128 and SEW = 8, one register holds 16 elements (`VLMAX` = 16). To process a list of 784 numbers the program
loops: each pass asks `vsetvli` for the number still left (AVL) and gets `vl` = 16, except the last pass which gets the
remainder. For 784 = 49 × 16 there are 49 passes and no remainder; for 1,030 elements the last pass would have `vl` = 6.

Instructions have the suffix of their operand form: `.vv` = vector and vector, `.vx` = vector and a scalar register,
`.vi` = vector and a 5-bit immediate, `.vs` = vector and a scalar kept in element 0 of a vector, `.v` = unit-stride memory
operand, `.wi`/`.wx` = the first operand is twice as wide (narrowing). Vector registers of double width use an **even/odd
register pair** (for example `v2`/`v3`).

### 6.2 The instructions this vector unit executes

`vd` = destination, `vs1`/`vs2` = source vector registers, `rs1` = scalar register, `i` = element number.

**Configuration**

| Instruction | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `vsetvli rd, rs1, vtype` | Set SEW and LMUL from `vtype`; `vl = min(x[rs1], VLMAX)`; write `vl` to `rd` | `vsetvli t0, a0, e8, m1` |
| `vsetivli rd, uimm, vtype` | The same with a 5-bit constant as AVL | `vsetivli t0, 16, e8, m1` |
| `vsetvli zero, zero, vtype` | Change SEW and keep the current `vl` | `vsetvli zero, zero, e32, m1` |

Legal settings: LMUL = 1 and SEW = 8, 16 or 32. Any other setting is ignored if it reaches the vector unit, and the decoder
flags it as illegal before that.

**Loads and stores (unit stride: consecutive elements)**

| Instruction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `vle8.v vd, (rs1)` | Load `vl` bytes from address rs1 into `vd` (elements of 8 bits) |
| `vle32.v vd, (rs1)` | Load `vl` words of 32 bits |
| `vse8.v vs3, (rs1)` | Store `vl` bytes; the other bytes of memory are not changed |
| `vse32.v vs3, (rs1)` | Store `vl` words |

The address is treated as 16-byte aligned (the low 4 address bits are ignored). Elements beyond `vl` are not touched.

**Arithmetic (SEW = 32 or 8)**

| Instruction | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `vadd.vv vd, vs2, vs1` | vd[i] = vs2[i] + vs1[i] | `vadd.vv v4, v2, v3` |
| `vadd.vx vd, vs2, rs1` | vd[i] = vs2[i] + x[rs1] (add a bias) | `vadd.vx v4, v2, a1` |
| `vsra.vi vd, vs2, imm` | vd[i] = vs2[i] >> imm, arithmetic (sign kept); the shift amount is masked to log2(SEW) bits | `vsra.vi v4, v2, 7` |
| `vsra.vx vd, vs2, rs1` | the same with the shift amount in a scalar register | `vsra.vx v4, v2, a2` |
| `vmax.vx vd, vs2, rs1` | vd[i] = max(vs2[i], x[rs1]), signed. With rs1 = x0 this is **ReLU** | `vmax.vx v4, v2, x0` |

**Widening multiply and reduction**

| Instruction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `vwmul.vv vd, vs2, vs1` | vd[i] = vs2[i] × vs1[i] with SEW = 8 inputs and **16-bit** results, written to the register pair `vd`/`vd+1` (`vd` must be even). The case −128 × −128 = 16,384 is correct |
| `vwredsum.vs vd, vs2, vs1` | vd[0] = vs1[0] + the sum of the 16-bit elements `i < vl` of the pair `vs2`/`vs2+1`, as a **32-bit** sum with no overflow (up to 784 elements) |

Note: in this design `vwredsum.vs` reads 16-bit source elements while SEW = 8. This differs from the standard (where the
source width equals SEW). The reference firmware for Spike therefore uses two standard 16-bit reductions; the results are identical.

**Narrowing**

| Instruction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `vnclip.wi vd, vs2, imm` | Shift each element of `vs2` right by `imm` with rounding (round to nearest, ties up) and **saturate** to the narrower type: 32 → 16 bits ([−32,768, 32,767]) or 16 → 8 bits ([−128, 127]) |
| `vnclip.wx vd, vs2, rs1` | the same with the shift amount in a scalar register |

The shift uses 5 bits (32 → 16) or 4 bits (16 → 8). Two `vnclip` steps (32 → 16 → 8) turn an INT32 sum back into INT8.

**Moves**

| Instruction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `vmv.v.x vd, rs1` | Copy the scalar x[rs1] to all `vl` elements of `vd` (broadcast) |
| `vmv.s.x vd, rs1` | Write the scalar to element 0 of `vd` (used as the start value of a reduction) |
| `vmv.x.s rd, vs2` | Read element 0 of `vs2` into a scalar register, sign-extended to 32 bits |

**Not supported (illegal and halting):** `vsetvl`, unsigned or scalar-operand widening forms (`vwmulu`, `vwredsumu`,
`vwmul.vx`), `vadd.vi`, `vsra.vv`, `vmax.vv`, `vnclip.wv`, `vmv.v.v`, `vmv.v.i`, masked forms (mask register `v0`), 16-bit
loads and stores (`vle16`, `vse16`), strided, indexed (gather/scatter), segment, whole-register and fault-only-first memory
instructions, floating point, LMUL above 1.

### 6.3 Worked example: one neuron of layer 1

The firmware computes one output of the first layer (a dot product of 784 inputs and 784 weights, then bias, ReLU and
narrowing):

```
        # a1 = address of the 784 image bytes, a2 = address of this neuron's 784 weights
        vsetivli t0, 1, e32, m1        # one element of 32 bits
        vmv.s.x  v8, x0                #   accumulator (element 0 of v8) = 0
        addi     t1, x0, 49            # 49 passes of 16 bytes
loop:   vsetivli t0, 16, e8, m1        # vl = 16 bytes
        vle8.v   v1, (a1)              # 16 pixels
        vle8.v   v2, (a2)              # 16 weights
        vwmul.vv v4, v1, v2            # 16 products of 16 bits -> v4/v5
        vwredsum.vs v8, v4, v8         # v8[0] += sum of the 16 products (32 bits)
        addi     a1, a1, 16
        addi     a2, a2, 16
        addi     t1, t1, -1
        bne      t1, x0, loop
        vmv.x.s  t2, v8                # t2 = the 32-bit sum
        add      t2, t2, a3            # + bias of the neuron
        # shift (requantize), then ReLU and narrow to INT8 with vnclip/vmax in the vector unit
```

(The listing is illustrative: it shows the idea, and a real assembler may also want the policy flags `ta, ma` at the end of `vsetvli`/`vsetivli`. The real code is in `src/sw/fw/mnist_fw.S`.) The scalar core runs the loop counter and
addresses; the vector unit does 16 multiplications and a 16-term sum per pass.

---

## 7. What the processor can do (capabilities)

| Capability | Value | How it is known |
|---|---|---|
| General computation | Anything that fits RV32I + `mul`: control code, integer math, loops, tables, simple protocols | The instruction set above |
| Parallel arithmetic | 16 INT8 products or 4 INT32 additions per vector instruction (VLEN 128) | VLEN and 4 lanes |
| Program size | 32 KB = 8,192 instructions | Memory map |
| Data size | 256 KB; the MNIST network uses about 100 KB of weights | Memory map and the network size |
| Clock | 200 MHz target; Fmax about 218 MHz after synthesis on the Arria 10 | `schemas/ppa_report.json` |
| Throughput measured | The slowest of 100 images took 252,418 cycles, about 1.26 ms at 200 MHz, so roughly 790 images per second | System test TC-057 (the time is computed from the cycle count) |
| Input / output | Memory loaded by a host; result on pins `o_result_label`, `o_sts_done`, and as a character on the UART serial line | Section 4 |
| Fixed-point only | INT8/INT16/INT32; no floating point | The vector subset |

It **cannot**: run an operating system (no interrupts, no privileged mode), divide, run floating-point code, run
convolution networks efficiently (no strided or masked vector loads), or hold models above 256 KB.

## 8. Applications

The same pattern, "load small integers, multiply in parallel, sum, rescale", is the heart of many small machine-learning
and signal-processing tasks. With other weights and layer sizes (and other firmware) the processor can be used for the
following. The sizes are estimates from the memory and speed above, not measured results.

| Application | What the processor does | Fit |
|---|---|---|
| **Handwritten digit recognition** (the example) | One 28 × 28 image through a 784 → 128 → 10 network | Done in the example |
| **Meter and display digit reading**, keypad or form digit entry | The same network on small digit images | Good: same size |
| **Keyword or sound-event detection** | A feature vector of a few hundred INT8 values (for example audio spectrum bands) through a small MLP | Good: the model fits in 256 KB, feature extraction would be added in firmware |
| **Sensor classification**: gesture, vibration, anomaly, activity | Features from an accelerometer or current sensor, a small MLP, a class number | Good: small inputs, low rate |
| **Small signal processing**: FIR filters, correlations, checksums | A dot product of a window with coefficients (`vwmul` + `vwredsum`) | Good for INT8/INT16 data |
| **Teaching and research** | A readable RISC-V core with a vector unit for courses, FPGA labs and to study AI-generated RTL | Good: 38 short modules, 59 passing tests |
| **Low-power edge devices** | Run a model on demand and stop; the result goes to the UART or to pins | Fits the design style; power was not analyzed |
| **Larger vision models** (convolutional networks, images above 28 × 28) | — | Not a fit: no convolution support, small memory |

## 9. Example application: reading a handwritten digit

The firmware `src/sw/fw/mnist_fw.S` runs the network **784 → 128 (ReLU) → 10** on one 28 × 28 grey-scale image.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Input | 784 INT8 pixels (49 vectors of 16) |
| Layer 1 | 128 neurons, weights 784 × 128 = 100,352 bytes |
| Layer 2 | 10 neurons, weights 128 × 10 = 1,280 bytes |
| Quantization | symmetric, one scale per tensor, INT8 weights and activations, INT32 bias and accumulator, scale a power of two so that requantization is a shift |
| Output | the largest of the 10 logits, a digit 0 to 9 |

**Sequence on the chip**

1. A host (or the testbench) holds the reset, loads the program, the weights and the image through the host load port, and releases the reset.
2. It raises `i_start_req`; `ctrl.start` becomes 1; the program clears it and sets `sts.busy`.
3. Layer 1 (128 neurons × 49 passes) and layer 2 (10 neurons × 8 passes) run on the vector unit; the scalar core finds the largest of the 10 logits.
4. The program writes `result.label`, sets `sts.done`, clears `sts.busy` and sends `'0' + label` over the UART.
5. The host reads `o_result_label`, `o_sts_done`, the `cycles` register and, if wanted, the logits through the host port.

Example: if the image is a "7", the logit of class 7 is the largest, `result.label` = 7 and the UART sends the character `7`.

## 10. Results and what they do not show

Numbers reported by the flow (`reports/`, `schemas/`); they were not re-run for this README.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Requirements | 87 (`schemas/structured_spec.json`) |
| RTL | 38 modules, 7,306 lines; Verible format and style lint clean; Verilator lint 0 warnings |
| Simulation | 60 tests planned; 59 run and **59 pass** (VCS). The one not run, TC-053, applies only to `PARA_VLEN` = 256 |
| System test | TC-057 runs 100 images; slowest 252,418 cycles |
| FPGA (Quartus Prime Pro 25.1, **after synthesis only**) | WNS +0.416 ns at 200 MHz (Fmax ≈ 218 MHz), 8,690 ALMs (2 % of the device), 6,646 registers, 10 DSP blocks, 2.36 Mbit of block memory |

What these numbers do **not** show:

- The network uses **synthetic placeholder weights and images** (question PRE1): no trained MNIST export was supplied. The
  59/59 pass is a **bit-exact comparison with the golden model**, not a measured recognition accuracy; the 96 % target of
  the intent was not measured. Real weights can be used with `MODEL=<file>.npz`.
- The FPGA result is **after synthesis only** (`implemented: false`): no place-and-route, hold slack not judged, nothing run on a board.
- Review gates and questions were approved automatically, so no person reviewed the decisions.
- ASIC synthesis was not run (no target library); DFT, power intent and physical design are out of scope.

| Folder | Holds |
|---|---|

Q3TUI's internal state (`.q3tui/`) and tool output (`build/`) are not included.

## 12. Running it again

With Q3TUI installed, in this folder:

```sh
q3tui tools init     # or adapt config/tools.json to your machine (tool paths, license server)
q3tui                # the terminal UI; or `q3tui auto` for the full unattended run
```

The firmware and the golden data alone can be rebuilt with
`make -C src/sw PROG_DIR=<dir> RISCV_PREFIX=<prefix> SPIKE=<spike>` (set `MODEL=<file>.npz` for real weights; `SPIKE_CHECK=0`
skips the cross-check with Spike). Simulation needs VCS and the FPGA flow needs Quartus; neither is in this folder.

## 13. Limits and notes

- One image at a time; no batch, no convolution, no training.
- No interrupts, exceptions or privilege levels; no `div`/`rem`; no CSR instructions in the firmware.
- One vector instruction at a time, LMUL = 1, no masking, no floating point.
- The PCIe wrapper that would drive the host load port on a board and a UART bootloader are not included.
- Machine-specific paths and the license server were removed; `config/tools.json` needs your tool paths.
- Generated file headers name `VLSIT - Q3TUI` as the author.
